title: Alfajores
subtitle: Shortbread biscuits sandwiched with dulce de leche
excerpt: Melt-in-the-mouth cornflour shortbread sandwiched with dulce de leche and rolled in desiccated coconut. This recipe makes 16 alfajores and takes about 1 hour 15 minutes including chilling time. They are the most beloved biscuit in Argentina and taste better the day after they are made.
sourceNotes: Alfajores trace their roots to Moorish confectionery brought to Spain, where they were made with honey and spices. In Argentina, dulce de leche replaced the original filling and the biscuits became a beloved national sweet. Argentina produces hundreds of commercial alfajores brands, with Havanna and Jorgito among the most recognised.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the baked, unfilled biscuits for up to 2 months. Defrost fully and fill with dulce de leche on the day.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The dough can be made 2 days ahead and refrigerated. The assembled alfajores taste better the following day once the dulce de leche has softened the biscuit slightly.

glossaryTerms.definition: A thick, golden caramel made by slowly cooking sweetened milk until the sugars caramelise. It is used throughout Latin America as a spread, filling and topping, and is central to Argentine baking and desserts.

content.text: This recipe makes 16 alfajores and takes about 1 hour 15 minutes including the 30-minute chill for the dough. The biscuits are delicate and very short thanks to the high proportion of cornflour, which is what gives them their characteristic crumbly texture. Handle them gently once baked.

items.prepNote: tin cooked into dulce de leche, or 300g shop-bought dulce de leche

content.text: Beat the butter and caster sugar together until pale and fluffy, about 3 minutes. Add the 2 egg yolks and a few drops of vanilla extract, then mix again until combined.
Sift together the plain flour, 150g cornflour and 1 tsp baking powder. Add to the butter mixture and mix on low until a soft dough forms. Wrap in cling film and refrigerate for 30 minutes.
Heat the oven to 160C (140C fan). Line 2 baking trays with baking paper.
On a lightly floured surface, roll the dough to 5mm thick. Cut out rounds using a 5cm cutter. You should get about 32 biscuits to make 16 sandwiches.

Bake for 10 to 12 minutes until the biscuits are just set and very lightly coloured on the base. They should not take on much colour on top. Cool on the tray for 5 minutes, then transfer carefully to a wire rack. They are very fragile while warm.

Once completely cool, spread a generous teaspoon of dulce de leche on the flat side of half the biscuits. Sandwich with the remaining biscuits. Roll the edges in icing sugar or desiccated coconut. Store in a tin at room temperature for up to 3 days.

attrs.cause: The dough was too warm when rolled, or the biscuits were moved too soon after baking
attrs.fix: Make sure the dough is properly chilled before rolling. Leave biscuits on the tray for at least 5 minutes before moving. Handle very gently; they firm up as they cool completely.

attrs.symptom: Biscuits spread too much and are thin
attrs.cause: Butter was too warm, or the dough was not chilled
attrs.fix: Start with softened but not melted butter. If the kitchen is warm, chill the rolled and cut biscuits on the tray for 15 minutes before baking.

attrs.cause: Dulce de leche is too warm or too runny
attrs.fix: Chill the dulce de leche before using. Use a teaspoon rather than a heaped tablespoon; alfajores are meant to have a thin, even layer of filling rather than a large dollop.

content.text: Alfajores are sold at every kiosk and supermarket in Argentina. The premium brand Havanna alfajores are considered a national treasure and are carried home as gifts from Buenos Aires. Homemade alfajores are a common birthday gift and bake sale staple. They taste better the next day once the dulce de leche has had time to soften the biscuit.
